# Warehouse fire disrupts Thornfield Junction freight corridor

A fire broke out shortly after dawn last Tuesday inside Warehouse 6 at the Thornfield
Junction freight yard, the transfer point where road shipments bound for the northern
coast are handed off to rail. The building, a 40,000-square-metre cross-dock structure
packed with palletised consumer goods, was fully involved within twenty minutes. Flames
reached the roof trusses before the yard's own suppression system could contain them, and
nothing of the structure remains standing above the foundation slab.

Kestrahaven Logistics leases Warehouse 6 from the yard's landowner and uses it as the sole
transfer point for shipments moving between its road fleet and the Meridian Rail
Consortium's northern spur line. The two organisations share the yard under a decade-old
handling agreement: Kestrahaven stages containers on the dock apron, and Meridian's crews
load them onto northbound consists three times a day. That arrangement has been the
backbone of the coastal supply chain since the yard opened, moving everything from
packaged food to household appliances toward the port towns that have no direct rail
access of their own.

The fire did not stay inside Warehouse 6. Radiant heat buckled two hundred metres of
Meridian's own track bed running along the warehouse's eastern wall, warping the rails
enough that trains can no longer pass over that section. A signal relay hut belonging to
Meridian, positioned twelve metres from the warehouse's loading dock, also burned, taking
out the block signalling for the entire northern spur. Without that signalling, Meridian
cannot safely run trains through Thornfield Junction at all, which means the disruption
now extends well past Kestrahaven's own operation and into the rail consortium's broader
network.

Emergency crews from three neighbouring districts responded, working through the morning
to keep the fire from reaching an adjacent fuel depot used by the yard's forklift fleet.
Water tenders drew from the yard's retention pond, which held enough capacity to keep the
depot cool without evacuating the wider industrial park. Workers on the morning shift at
Warehouse 6 evacuated through the eastern loading doors before the roof began to fail;
none were still inside when the structure collapsed.

Kestrahaven's road fleet has since been rerouted to a smaller overflow yard eleven
kilometres south, a facility never designed to handle the volume Warehouse 6 processed.
Drivers report queues stretching past the overflow gate through most of the day, and
several coastal grocers have already begun sourcing perishables from alternate
distributors rather than wait for a transfer point that no longer functions at its usual
throughput. Meridian, for its part, has redirected its three daily northbound consists
onto a longer route that bypasses the damaged spur entirely, adding several hours to each
run and pushing scheduled arrivals at the port towns later into the evening than the
timetable Meridian has kept for years.

The warehouse itself held goods belonging to several of Kestrahaven's shipping clients,
including packaged foodstuffs nearing their sell-by window and a shipment of household
appliances destined for a coastal retail chain. Both categories were stored in the
building's southern bay, which took the worst of the fire and where nothing is expected to
be salvageable. Kestrahaven's insurers have been notified of the loss, and the company has
begun the process of identifying which client shipments were destroyed outright versus
which were staged elsewhere in the yard and survived.

The roof trusses failed in a series of loud, spaced-out cracks as sections gave way one
after another, audible from the row of houses backing onto the yard's northern fence.
Smoke from the fire was visible from the coastal highway for most of the morning, and the
plume drifted east over open farmland rather than toward the nearest town, so the town's
air quality monitors never recorded the kind of spike that would trigger a
shelter-in-place notice.

No timeline exists yet for reopening the northern spur, and no decision has been made on
whether Warehouse 6 will be rebuilt on the same footprint or relocated elsewhere in the
yard. Both companies continue to operate the rest of their shared footprint at Thornfield
Junction, including the western dock apron that the fire never reached.
